newsitem.title: UK: Copper rides out storm on LME, still ends weak.
newsitem.headline: Copper rides out storm on LME, still ends weak.

text.p: Copper prices managed to stage a mini-rally during late Wednesday LME trading, although the market still closed easier after hitting seven-week lows earlier.
Other markets were affected by the turmoil in copper, although aluminium and zinc defended downside levels and eventually closed little changed.
Traders attributed copper's latest losses to another wave of speculative selling, sell-stops, and option-related sales.
Short-term fundamentals remain supportive, however, and the cash/threes backwardation, which wobbled at one stage, still ended over $100.
"This market is still tight in July/August...there is not that much stock around, so any sort of disruption will impact on the market," analyst Martin Squires of LME trader Rudolf Wolff said.
Copper's low-point was $2,355, which at that stage was over nine percent below the highs near $2,600 that prevailed only last Friday.
"It held near $2,350, where there is good support. Then there was some bargain-hunting and profit-taking buying," Squires said.
Last three months business was at $2,373 a tonne, still down a hefty $64 from Tuesday's kerb close.
In the short-term an oversold market could well consolidate and rally a little higher, although current volatility makes this unpredictable.
"The only certainty is that it will be uncertain," a trader said.
Elsewhere, nerves were on edge at one stage when copper was in free-fall, before late buying ensured closing levels in some markets were not far adrift of Tuesday.
"The funds tried to bully aluminium down and get it below the $1,550 level," Squires said.
However, trade buying checked the fall, and the market was able to rally back to $1,569, down just $8 from the previous kerb.
Zinc's action was similar, with a lack of followthrough selling on the downside prompting a reversal. By the close prices were challenging $1,400 once more, ending at $1,396, down just $1.
Nickel was on tenterhooks for developments at the Inco Sudbury strike talks, but nevertheless fell away. Last trade was at $7,050, down $120.
Lead was $2 softer at $618, while tin shed $15 to $5,565 a tonne. Alloy was quoted at a slightly lower $1,460/65.
